To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
in females, but not in males, the expression of genes involved in the pathophysiology of PD appears to be associated with the blood levels of some PCB congeners, especially non-coplanar congeners.

(1) non-coplanar (non-planar) PCBs are associated with the expression levels of PD-associated genes in female blood cells, (2) the expression levels of 131 genes are affected by increasing levels of PCBs, (3) 39 of the genes affected by PCBs are also affected in the substantia nigr of PD patients, (4) the expression levels are affected in a manner similar to the PD-specific genes affected in the brain of PD patients
PCB exposure is associated with expression changes of PD-related genes in the blood of females, but not in males.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of a group of genes that are both PD-specific and sensitive to PCB exposure in blood cells.
the first study of the association between the expression levels of PD-associated genes in blood and exposure to PCBs.
the first evidence of a link between PCBs and PD in human subjects.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the observed gene expression changes in females are likely to reflect the effect of PCB exposure on the dopaminergic system, and not a risk factor for PD.

PCBs are not directly involved in the etiology of sporadic PD, but that the observed association between PCB exposure levels and PD-specific gene expression levels in blood cells may be an indicator of a more complex interaction between PCB exposure and the occurrence of PD.
PCBs may be linked to PD, but only in female subjects.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the expression levels of PD-related genes in blood cells from healthy females are associated with the blood levels of noncoplanar PCBs, which may be linked to the risk of developing PD.
the expression levels of PD-associated genes in the blood of PCB-exposed females appear to be associated in an increasing manner with PCB exposure.
non-coplanar and coplanar PCBs are associated with PD-specific genes expression levels in females, and that this association is not observed in males.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the association between PCBs in blood and PD-specific gene expression in blood cells is gender-specific.
the expression levels of a large set of PD-specific genes appear to be affected by increasing levels of PCBs in blood.
non-coplanar environmental PCBs may be associated with the occurrence of PD in females.
